text: Key takeaways Choose on method and transparency, not on promises. A credible GEO agency shows how it picks prompts, what it will change on your site, how it measures and what it cannot control. Test claims yourself. Run the buyer prompts in several engines, repeat them, and ask for a dated baseline and retest. One screenshot proves nothing. Get scope, exclusions, access, measurement and exit terms in writing. Walk away from anyone who promises citations or rankings. Why is choosing a GEO agency harder than choosing an SEO agency? Because the field is young, results are less certain, and there is no shared standard for what the work includes. In SEO you can check rankings. In GEO the answer you see may not be the answer your buyer sees, and no agency controls what AI engines say. You have to judge method and honesty instead of outcomes. Three facts explain the difficulty. First, answers vary. SparkToro and Gumshoe.ai found in January 2026, across nearly 3,000 runs of 12 prompts by 600 volunteers, that the odds of getting the same list of brands twice were under 1 in 100 ( AI recommendation lists rarely repeat , Search Engine Land, January 2026). A single "we got you into ChatGPT " screenshot is close to meaningless. Second, definitions differ. One agency means a report, another means page rewrites, another means digital PR. Third, tools are marketed as services, and services as tools, so the label tells you little. Google adds a caution that applies to everyone selling in this space. Its guidance, updated in July 2026, says no third party tool has access to Google's internal ranking or AI systems, so any tool's claims should be checked against official guidance, and it calls optimizing for generative AI search still SEO ( Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search , Google Search Central, July 2026). You do not need to agree with every word. But it tells you that the honest position is modest. We are a GEO agency, so read this with that in mind. We wrote it as we would want a buyer to read it: to help you filter out weak offers, including ours if ours is weak for you. For context on what the work is, see the generative engine optimization overview, and for what a typical engagement contains, what a GEO company does. What should a GEO agency actually do for you? It should do six things: measure where you stand, fix access and technical issues, make priority pages answer ready, align your brand facts, work on credible mentions beyond your site, and report honestly. If an agency covers fewer, ask which ones it expects you to do. Baseline. Test a set of real buyer prompts across several engines, repeated, with dates. Without it there is nothing to compare against. Technical access. Check that the crawlers behind AI answers can reach your pages: OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, Claude-SearchBot, Googlebot, Bingbot and others, at robots.txt and CDN level. See technical GEO . Page rewrites. Restructure priority pages with direct answers, headings that match real questions, evidence and accurate FAQs. Entity and facts. Make names, addresses, services and claims consistent everywhere. Authority. Reviews, directories, press and communities that engines draw on. Slow and category specific. Reporting. Repeated measurement, mentions and citations separately, and a next step list. A useful test: ask for a description of week one, week two and week three. A real provider can say what happens on each day. A vague one answers in adjectives. Our own scope for the GEO Pilot is written that way on purpose: week 1 baseline and audit, week 2 technical fixes, week 3 up to 10 priority pages made answer ready, week 4 retest, report and a 90 day roadmap. Which 12 questions should you ask any GEO agency? Ask all twelve, in writing if you can, and compare the answers between providers. What you want is specific answers with named steps. Evasion is also information. 1. How do you decide which prompts matter? Good answer: they collect real buyer questions from your sales calls, support tickets, search data and customers, group them by intent, and agree the list with you before testing. They freeze the list and version any change. Poor answer: they run "your keywords" through a tool, or generate prompts by asking a model. See how to research buyer prompts for what good looks like. 2. How do you measure results, and how often do you retest? Good answer: a baseline on the same prompts, repeated runs per engine, an appearance rate with the numerator and denominator, mentions and citations reported separately, and dated notes of engine changes. SparkToro's work suggests position is unreliable and share of responses is steadier. Poor answer: one score, one screenshot, or "we monitor continuously" with no method. Our GEO reporting template shows a defensible layout. 3. What exactly will you change on my site? Good answer: a written list by item, such as robots.txt rules, sitemap, canonicals, structured data, specific pages and sections, with the approval path. Poor answer: "optimise your content for AI". Ask whether they edit your site or send recommendations, because the price and your workload differ. 4. How do you handle AI crawlers? Good answer: they name the bots and their purposes, and separate search from training. OpenAI documents OAI-SearchBot for ChatGPT search and GPTBot for training, and says each setting is independent ( Overview of OpenAI crawlers , OpenAI, accessed October 2026). Anthropic separates ClaudeBot, Claude-SearchBot and Claude-User. Perplexity separates PerplexityBot from Perplexity-User. An agency that tells you to block or allow "all AI bots" without that distinction is guessing. See what to allow in robots.txt . 5. What do you not control, and what do you not promise? Good answer: they say plainly that they do not control engine answers, cannot promise citations, rankings or traffic, and that engines change. Google's John Mueller said in 2025 that if an SEO promises rankings or search traffic, "that's usually a red flag" ( Google's advice on hiring an SEO , Search Engine Journal, July 2025). The same applies to AI answers. Poor answer: any guarantee. 6. Who will do the work, and how senior are they? Good answer: named people, their roles, and who you talk to each week. Ask who writes the page rewrites and who reviews technical changes. Poor answer: a pitch from a senior person and delivery by juniors you never meet, or a pipeline of unreviewed machine generated copy. 7. What is in scope, what is out and what does it cost? Good answer: a written scope list, written exclusions, a price tied to scope and a clear statement of how ongoing work is priced. Poor answer: a number with no scope. The article on how much GEO costs goes through the factors that should move a price. 8. Can you show real work, and what can you tell me about it? Good answer: a client case with the market, the starting point, what was changed, what was measured and what the limits of the evidence are. Names may be confidential. The method should not be. Poor answer: logos, vague percentages, or screenshots with no dates. For reference, our public proof is limited to two cases: Emtech , a Dubai IT company cited for IT AMC queries across five engines, and Sudarshan Stoneix , a marble and granite company with a six month result measured by a third party tool. One client and one market each. Not a promise. 9. How do you work with my existing team and vendors? Good answer: they describe a workflow with your developers, content team and any SEO provider, including how they avoid contradicting each other. Poor answer: they want exclusive control of your site, or they dismiss your other vendors. 10. How do you handle compliance and accuracy? Good answer: a review step for regulated claims, a process for subject matter sign off, and a rule against inventing statistics or testimonials. Ask about health, finance and legal content in particular. Poor answer: no review, or "AI writes it, we publish it". 11. What do I own at the end, and how do I leave? Good answer: you own the prompt set, reports, page edits and any content created, with exports in usable formats and a notice period. Poor answer: your data lives in their tool, or the contract auto renews with penalties. 12. What would make you tell me not to buy? Good answer: a real list. For example, your buyers do not use AI tools to research your category, your site has serious basic problems, or you have no clear offer. An agency that can never say no is selling, not advising. Work What actually changes What will you change on my site? Who does the work? How do you work with my team? Terms What you get and keep What is in and out of scope? What do I own at the end? How do I leave? Honesty Limits and proof What do you not control? Can you show real work? When would you tell me not to buy? The twelve questions in this article, grouped. What are the red flags when hiring a GEO agency? Ten red flags, each with the reason it matters. One alone may be a misunderstanding. Three together is a pattern. Promised citations, rankings or traffic. Nobody controls AI answers. A "proprietary" method that cannot be explained. Real GEO work is mostly access, structure, facts and credible mentions. A single AI visibility score. If the formula is hidden you cannot audit it. Proof from one screenshot. Answers change run to run. Long contracts before any baseline. Twelve months of commitment on trust alone. Mass produced content. Hundreds of near identical pages. Google's July 2026 guide asks for original, non commodity content. Fake mentions or link schemes. Google says seeking artificial mentions across the web is not effective, and it can create risk. No technical work. If they never mention crawler access, indexing or rendering, they may skip the layer everything else depends on. Blocking or allowing every bot. It shows the agency does not separate search from training. Pressure. "The window is closing" is a sales line. Engines change, but not in a week. A fair caution about red flags. A single odd answer is not proof of bad faith. Some agencies use different words for the same good practice. Ask a follow up before you rule anyone out. How can you test a GEO agency's claims yourself? You can test most claims in an afternoon, with no special tools. This is the strongest protection you have. Write your own prompts. Take 10 real questions your buyers ask. Do not use the agency's list. Run them in several engines. ChatGPT with search on, Google AI Mode, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude and Copilot if relevant. Use a clean session and note the location. Run each three times. Save the answer text and the sources shown, with the date. Check the claim against your data. If an agency says a client is "cited in ChatGPT", run the prompt yourself three times. Do the same for any reference account you can access. Check access. Use the AI crawler access checker on your own site and ask the agency to explain each result. Check the sources they cite. Do the studies exist, are they dated, and do they say what the agency claims? For instance, the GEO research paper by Aggarwal and colleagues (KDD 2024) reports visibility gains of up to 40 percent in its tests and that keyword stuffing underperformed a baseline ( GEO: Generative Engine Optimization , Aggarwal et al., KDD 2024, August 2024). That is a research result under defined conditions, not a promise for your site. An agency that quotes "40 percent" as a guaranteed uplift misreads it. Ask for a free baseline sample. A short sample of five prompts shows how they think. The free AI Visibility Checker gives you a first look to compare against. Pay attention to how the agency reacts to being tested. Good providers welcome it. They know answers vary and they want you to understand why. What does fair proof of GEO results look like? Fair proof is dated, specific, repeatable and honest about its limits. It does not claim that the agency alone caused the result. Look for these five elements: A named prompt set and the engines tested. A baseline and a retest on the same prompts, with dates and run counts. Mentions and citations separately. Semrush's 2026 AI Visibility Index found that fewer than half of the top 100 mentioned brands also appeared in the matching top 100 cited domains, so reports that blur them hide information (Semrush, October 2026). See the mention and citation gap . A change log. What was altered and when, so you can see what might explain a shift. A limits statement. Other things changed at the same time, engines update, and the sample is a sample. Be careful with traffic claims. Conductor's 2026 benchmark found AI referral traffic was 1.08 percent of total website traffic across 10 industries, with ChatGPT driving 87.4 percent of AI referrals (Conductor, 2026). An agency promising big traffic from AI is promising something the averages do not support. And Pew Research Center found users clicked a link inside a Google AI summary in only 1 percent of visits to pages with one (Pew Research Center, July 2025). Influence without a click is real but hard to prove, so honest reports use leads with self reported source and brand search alongside visits. Beware of attributing too neatly. Ahrefs found branded web mentions correlated with AI Overview brand visibility at 0.664 in a study of 75,000 brands, and states correlation is not causation (Ahrefs, May 2025). A before and after chart does not show cause. Good proof says so. Reading proof From weak to strong evidence Weak proof Strong proof One screenshot Logos and vague percentages Dated baseline and retest Repeated runs plus a change log and limits A guide to weighing proof, not measured data. How do GEO agency pricing models work? Three models cover most offers: a fixed project, a monthly retainer and tools you run yourself. The right one depends on your capacity and how sure you are about the work needed. A fixed project suits a first engagement: a known cost, a known end date, and a baseline you can judge. A retainer suits ongoing content, authority and monitoring work, once a baseline shows what is worth continuing. Tools alone suit teams with skill and time who need measurement. We cover the logic of each, the hidden costs and a staged budget in how much GEO costs, and the options by job in types of AI visibility tools. Two rules of thumb. Do not pay a large retainer before a baseline exists. And do not choose purely on the lowest price: a low fee for vague work costs more than a higher fee for clear work. Our own entry offer is the GEO Pilot , $999 USD, one time, inside 30 days. Ongoing work after it is quoted, and the pricing page shows how. Should you hire an agency, a freelancer, an in house person or buy a tool? It depends on your capacity, speed and risk. There is no universal winner. Use these decision rules. Hire an agency if you need the technical, content and measurement work done together, you lack in house capacity, and you want a defined scope and timeline. Skip the agency if you have an experienced technical SEO lead, developers who respond and content writers who can do answer first writing. Add a tool for measurement. Hire a freelancer if the scope is narrow, for example a schema and robots.txt fix, or a few page rewrites, and you can manage the work. Hire in house if GEO will be a permanent function across many markets and you can recruit someone senior. Buy a tool if you only need measurement and you have someone to act on the findings. Do not buy one hoping it will do the fixing. Option Strength Risk Best when Agency Combined skills, defined scope Variable quality, cost You lack capacity Freelancer Flexible, lower cost Narrow skill, single point of failure Scope is small In house Deep context, permanent Slow to build, hard to hire Many markets, long term Tool only Cheap, always on Needs someone to act You have skilled staff Pricing choices Fixed project first Known cost and end date Baseline before any commitment Evidence decides the next step → Retainer first Spreads cost over months Suits ongoing content and authority work Risky before a baseline exists Both can be fair. Ask for written deliverables either way. What should a written scope or contract include? Eight items. Ask for them whatever you buy. They protect both sides. Scope list. Named deliverables, such as number of pages, audits, fixes and reports. "Optimisation" is not a line item. Exclusions. What is not included, such as a rebuild, link building, paid media or extra languages. Access and approvals. What access is needed, who approves changes and the expected response time. Measurement method. Engines, prompts, run counts, report dates and who keeps the raw answers. Ownership. You own the prompt set, reports, edits and new content. Term and exit. A short initial term, a notice period and no penalties for leaving. Accuracy and compliance. Sign off for regulated claims, no invented statistics or testimonials. No outcome promise. The contract should state that no ranking, citation or traffic result is promised. If the contract promises one, the contract is wrong. Example, hypothetical: how a buyer might run the process This is an invented scenario to show the steps, not a client result. A Dubai based B2B software firm wants to appear in AI answers for "compliance software for UAE banks". The marketing director shortlists three providers and sends each the same one page brief: the domain, the market, 15 buyer prompts, the engines that matter, the pages that matter most, and a request for a scope and price. Week 1. She reads the replies against the twelve questions. Provider A sends a long deck and a guarantee of "top citations in 90 days". She crosses it off. Provider B replies with a scoped plan: baseline, crawler audit, ten page rewrites, a retest, an itemised exclusion list, and no guarantee. Provider C is a tool vendor offering a dashboard and no implementation. Week 2. She runs her own 15 prompts three times in four engines and saves the results. She then asks Provider B to explain, for two of her pages, what they would change and why. The answers are specific: the pricing page has no figures, the robots.txt blocks an AI search bot, and two product names differ across the site. Week 3. She asks for the contract. It lists scope, exclusions, a 30 day term, report dates and her ownership of all outputs. Her legal team adds a review step for compliance claims. The agency agrees. Week 4 onward. Work starts. At day 30 she receives a before and after report on her own 15 prompts. It shows mentions and citations separately, notes what else changed, and lists next steps. She decides, with evidence, whether to continue. Notice that she never relied on a promise, and that the most useful steps cost her only a few hours: her own prompts, a clear brief and a written scope. When should you not hire a GEO agency, including us? Not yet if any of these apply. We would rather tell you than sell you. Your buyers do not use AI tools to research what you sell. Ask recent customers how they found you. Forrester reported in January 2026 that 94 percent of business buyers use AI in their buying process, and G2 found in April 2026 that 51 percent of B2B software buyers start research with an AI assistant more often than with Google (Forrester, January 2026; G2, April 2026). That is strong for software and business buying. It may be far weaker in your category. Your site has basic failures: it is often down, blocked or has no clear offer. Fix those first. You cannot approve changes in reasonable time. You want a promised outcome. You have one narrow need, such as a robots.txt fix. A freelancer or a free tool may be enough. Start with the robots.txt generator if so. If you are small, is GEO worth it for a small business helps you decide. What should you do this week? Do these before talking to any agency, including us. They take a few hours and improve every conversation. Write 10 to 15 real buyer questions. Use sales calls and support tickets. Run them in at least three engines, three times each. Save the results with dates. Run the free AI Visibility Checker and the AI crawler access checker. Write a one page brief: domain, markets, languages, key pages, who approves changes, and your budget range. Send it to two or three providers with the twelve questions. Compare in writing. Ask each for a sample baseline on five of your prompts. Choose on method and transparency. Sign a short first term. If you would like us to be one of the providers you compare, see the GEO Pilot, $999 USD, one time, inside 30 days, done for you on any platform, with a before and after report. You can also request an LLM visibility audit . We do not promise rankings, citations or traffic, and we would not trust anyone who does. text: 2 November 2026 In Conductor’s US benchmark , AI referrals accounted for 1.08% of all website visits across the industries studied. An agency’s impressive citation chart is therefore worth investigating, not accepting as evidence of business impact. Shortlist GEO agencies in three passes: verify their AI-answer evidence, audit how they measure questions your buyers ask, and test whether they can get changes approved and shipped. Compare contracts only after those capabilities are clear. No agency can promise a particular AI answer, so give every candidate the same requests and compare what you can inspect. GEO, short for generative engine optimization, is the work of getting a brand described accurately, cited and recommended in the answers of AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode. Onely, the AI search agency founded by Bartosz Góralewicz, uses AI search to connect brands to their audience and drive sales, so this Onely guide judges a GEO agency by whether its work reaches the people asking, not only by citation counts. We believe AI search is not about keywords anymore: it is about connecting to the audience across the questions they ask before they buy, and most agencies miss that because they are stuck in keywords. Our view at Onely is that a GEO agency earns the job by solving the customer journey, because AI search turned searching into a conversation instead of a keyword lookup. Onely is not the right hire for every company: we think it is the strongest choice for enterprises that want international AI search, and the conditions are set out in the section on who should hire Onely. Onely wrote and publishes this guide, so we are an interested party. The checks on this page work for judging any GEO agency, Onely included. How do you shortlist a GEO agency? Apply three gates before comparing pitches. First, request dated AI-answer results with the underlying prompts and responses. Second, examine the platforms, scoring rules, and buyer questions behind those results. Third, ask the agency to show how a recommendation would pass through your teams to publication and verification. Advance candidates that pass all three. In the first meeting, ask each GEO agency to define GEO in its own words: which AI surfaces it covers, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini and Perplexity, how the work relates to SEO and AEO (answer engine optimization), and what it will measure. A vague answer such as “we do everything for AI”, or a narrow one that reduces GEO to content writing or structured data alone, signals an immature service. Which five criteria should you apply to every candidate? Apply the same five criteria to every candidate, and record what each agency provides , not what it says it can provide. Criterion Ask each agency to provide What to check Past AI-answer results Dated baseline, follow-up, prompts, change log Do observations support the claim? Measurement Sample prompts, answers, citations, mentions Can you inspect scoring? Buyer fit Priority questions, competitors, success definitions Do prompts reflect decisions? Enterprise delivery Owners, approvals, access, verification Can changes ship and be checked? Commercial terms Scope, exclusions, review, handover Does the fee match the work? Send everyone the same request: a case-study evidence packet, a sample report, an initial on-site and off-site plan, a responsibility outline, and a proposed scope. Compare the buyer questions behind each prompt set and the actual answers and cited sources, rather than report rankings, mention totals, or polished screenshots. Ask to inspect how the report groups brands, topics, and prompts, and which answers and cited pages sit behind its totals. Conductor, which sells search software, documents those configurable elements in its AI Search Performance tool . An agency using another tool should explain its method just as clearly. A confidential case study can still qualify: request redacted answers, dates, methods, and a permitted reference or live method review. Then test delivery. One published comparison of enterprise SEO agencies, written by an agency that sells SEO services, scores each candidate on how it handles decisions and approvals across marketing, engineering, product, legal, brand and regional teams. Your shortlist should include agencies whose proposed work can move through your approval process. Which agencies belong on a GEO shortlist? The agencies that belong on a GEO shortlist are the ones that pass all three gates, whichever list or referral brought them to you. Many published lists of the best GEO and AI SEO agencies are written by agencies that place themselves on the list, so a high place on a list tells you who wrote it before it tells you who can do the work. What should you prepare before talking to agencies? Bring buyer questions, relevant competitors, accurate product claims, applicable compliance rules, and your definition of a qualified opportunity. Give candidates the same material and ask which questions they would test first. Which buyer questions belong in the first prompt set? Start with discovery, comparison, use-case, and purchase questions drawn from sales conversations, site search, and research your teams already have. In G2’s 2026 survey of B2B software buyers , comparing vendor strengths and weaknesses was the leading reason respondents used AI chatbots for software research. G2 sells software marketplace services; its finding gives you a practical test: will the prompt set reveal how an assistant compares you with a real alternative? Ask agencies to justify their choices. A question your buyers routinely ask deserves attention even if your brand performs poorly on it. For multiple markets, request market-specific questions as well as translations: buyers may compare different options or raise different concerns. What counts as a useful result for your business? Define what a good answer must get right. Does it describe your capabilities accurately and recommend you for a fitting use case? Does it merely mention you, or cite your page while recommending a competitor? Track those distinctions alongside visits and sales outcomes. One agency that sells GEO services proposes three separate measures: how often the brand is mentioned in AI answers for its category, how accurately those answers represent the brand, and how well AI-influenced sessions convert. Agree on the CRM stages and sales feedback you will use to identify qualified demand. Tell candidates which product, legal, and regional approvers must review claims before publication. How do you test an agency’s AI visibility evidence? Have each finalist walk through a dated baseline and follow-up for the same disclosed prompts and platforms. Inspect the responses, cited URLs, competitors, and scoring rules. Ask what changed on the site or elsewhere, when it changed, and what other activity coincided with the reported gain. How do you audit one sample report down to the answer? Audit one sample report by choosing one claimed improvement and following it back to the answers. Request the raw prompt, full responses, run dates, platform and model details where available, and cited URLs. Have the agency classify examples as brand mentions, AI citations, favorable recommendations, or competitor recommendations. Include ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, or Google AI Mode where they matter to your buyers. Ask why the prompts were chosen and how often checks repeat. Rerun selected questions during diligence; compare the new answers with the report. Botify, which sells AI visibility software, treats changing AI answers and unavailable query-volume data as reasons AI visibility reports are signals, not exhaustive market-share measurements . Require a justified schedule and a consistent comparison method. What does a case study establish, and what does it not? A case study can demonstrate an agency’s method. A useful one states the measured change, the period it covers, and how the agency mapped prompts and read the analytics behind it. Request the dated change log and answers alongside other marketing activity to assess what the agency’s work may have contributed. Accept necessary redaction, but require enough detail to examine the claim. Most published GEO case studies cannot pass that test. One agency directory studied 142 GEO case studies from 68 agencies: 66% named no AI platform, 27% reported no AI metric, only 5.6% gave before-and-after numbers, and only 13% tied AI search to leads or revenue. At Onely we read that as the gap to test for: a case study that never reaches leads or revenue shows that a brand was named, not that the work connected it to its audience and drove sales. Controlled GEO experiments by Aggarwal and coauthors found improved visibility for optimized sources against controls on Perplexity. The experiments support testing proposed changes and checking the resulting answers. What if dashboards and analytics disagree? Inspect the answers, then check each tool’s prompt coverage and referral classification. Semrush, which sells AI visibility software, describes share of voice, mention sentiment, and competitor coverage as distinct measures . seoClarity, which sells search software, reports that AI search traffic remains a small share of organic traffic in its client sample . Check absolute visits alongside visibility trends, then investigate whether either connects to qualified demand. A cited page that supports a competitor recommendation should not be scored like an answer that recommends your brand. Can the agency get the proposed work shipped across your teams? Ask for a short audit of your site and the outside sources shaping relevant answers. Botify and DemandSphere’s 2024 study of more than 120,000 keywords across 22 sites found AI Overviews could appear for up to 47% of the keywords studied, using methods that encouraged them to show; have the agency sample your relevant searches before prioritizing fixes. Trace one recommendation through owner, access, approval, publication, and verification to test cross-team delivery. What would the agency change on your site? Request prioritized findings on crawlability, accessible content, structured information, and whether key pages answer buyer questions clearly. For each finding, require a deliverable, an owner, and an acceptance check. One SEO agency’s published case study describes marking up questions and answers with FAQPage structured data. A usable recommendation would specify the page, proposed markup, publishing owner, and check of the live version. Ask which changes strengthen SEO foundations and which AI-answer hypotheses the agency will test afterward. BrightEdge, which sells search software, reports that the share of consideration-stage citations going to brand-owned pages differs across industries . The audit should reflect your sector and existing content rather than prescribe a publishing quota. Which outside sources shape the answer? Have the agency identify third-party pages that describe or compare your brand, check their accuracy, and prioritize sources your buyers use. In Ranqo’s observational audit across AI platforms , produced by the vendor, 2.9% of recorded citations pointed to the studied brand’s own site. Inspect the external sources in your answers before setting off-site priorities. Ask for the agency’s plan to keep the brand, its founders and its services described accurately and consistently across directories, wikis and the other knowledge sources AI answers draw on. Inconsistent entity information gives an assistant conflicting facts to choose between. Ask which corrections or legitimate earned mentions the agency would pursue through digital PR, who would contact each source, and how it would check the resulting answer. Microsoft describes prominent citations and linked passages in Copilot Search ; evaluate where those links lead and what the answer says about you. How do you follow one change from recommendation to verification? Follow one change by naming everyone it passes through: the agency lead; internal SEO, web, content, PR, and analytics owners; and the final approver. Ask who has CMS and measurement access, where approvals are recorded, who deploys the change, and how the report separates blocked work from published work. Approval delays can be the real bottleneck. One agency-selection guide, from a vendor that sells related services, recommends a paid pilot of four to six weeks with two or three finalists and puts analytics ownership and AI governance into the contract terms. Use a pilot to test handoffs through launch. Onely runs that route from the questions real customers ask: Audience Insights and Discovery finds those questions, Content Strategy for AI decides what each answer needs, and AI Optimization and Implementation makes the changes on the site and off it. Ask every candidate to demonstrate that full route. Which questions and contract terms should you check before signing? Compare what proposals include and what your teams must do. Put implementation responsibilities, review points, changes, termination, and handover in writing. Which commercial questions should you ask every finalist? Ask every finalist for an itemized scope covering the audit, prompt tracking, content, technical fixes, off-site work, reporting, and implementation. Identify exclusions and the access or approvals your teams must supply. Give each deliverable an observable acceptance check: an approved page, deployed fix, recorded answer check, or accessible report. One SEO agency’s guide to contracts advises specifying verifiable activities, implementation responsibilities, approvals, change control, and reporting rather than guaranteed positions. Pay for defined work the agency can perform and you can inspect. How do you compare a GEO agency’s fee against the work and your internal effort? Compare fees by setting implementation hours, tool costs, review demands, and exclusions alongside each one. A public price tells you what one offer includes; it gives little basis for comparing two different enterprise plans. A lower retainer may also leave more deployment and measurement work with your team. Onely has no rate card, and what we charge depends on how much audience research the brand needs, how new its problem is, and how many countries it sells in. Which review, change, and exit terms should you agree? Agree the first review point before work starts. Specify what happens when approval is delayed, how new work is priced, and what notice is required and what handover includes. Establish who retains the prompt set, raw answers, reporting access, produced assets, and implementation documentation after termination. Agiled, which sells business management software, includes deliverables, measurement tools, reporting, and handover in its SEO contract template . Analytics accounts, Search Console, business profiles and directory listings should be held in the brand’s name, and the contract should state that they stay with the brand if it parts ways with the agency. Before signing, ask: What is the success condition for the first phase? The answer should name shipped work and measurements you can inspect, even if AI answers do not move. Judge the first 90 days against a plan the agency commits to in writing: a baseline of AI answers in the first weeks, fixes shipping by around week four, and prompt-level movement reported by week twelve. A 90-day initial term, rather than a 12-month lock-in, keeps that plan testable before a long commitment. What are the red flags, and how will you check the hire worked? Challenge guaranteed placements, rankings-only reports, unexplained visibility scores, and plans built around a single tactic. Ask what each tactic adds to SEO foundations and which buyer-question answers will be checked afterward. Which claims should stop a pitch? BrightEdge, which sells SEO software, finds overlap between AI Overview citations and organic rankings . Ask a candidate showing rankings to demonstrate what the AI answer actually says. If it promises placement, ask which observed result would cause it to change its plan; controlled experiments show possible visibility improvements, not a guarantee for your brand. Stop a GEO pitch that relies on any of these claims: a special relationship with OpenAI or Google, a secret method the agency will not explain, mass production of low-quality pages, llms.txt or structured data sold as the whole GEO service, prompt injection or hidden manipulation, undisclosed paid coverage, a proprietary score with no raw data behind it, or instant placement, when citation growth typically takes two to three months of iterative work. Agency-selection advice differs on proof of success. One list of AI SEO agencies, written by an agency that sells AI SEO services, treats documented appearances and citations as the evidence of capability. Another, written by a content and SEO agency that ranks itself first, puts attributable pipeline and revenue ahead of screenshots. Require both answer-level proof and downstream measures where available. Review the work linking them before attributing a referral or opportunity to agency work. What should the first review establish? Return to the agreed prompts and change log. Separate published work from work awaiting approval; compare repeated answers with the baseline; and check accuracy, recommendation context, referrals, and sales feedback. If answers vary or qualified demand has not moved, record that result and choose the next hypothesis to test. Who should hire Onely as its GEO agency? Onely fits enterprises that want AI search to connect them to their audience in several countries, and it is not the best match for every company that runs these checks. Three conditions decide the fit. You need to connect to your audience. The prompt set should come from the questions your customers really ask in each market, not from a keyword list translated into questions. You need work built around your specific challenge. Your approvers, markets and existing content decide what can ship, so the plan has to be made for them rather than copied from another client. You need results, not old-school SEO metrics. The first review should show whether AI answers moved qualified demand, not only whether a visibility score went up. Onely is an AI search agency founded by Bartosz Góralewicz, with headquarters in Austin, Texas, and an office in Wrocław, Poland. Onely solves a bigger problem than GEO, a problem AI search created: brands show up in answers and still do not connect to their audience. Onely goes beyond keywords and beyond content optimization, towards the customer connection that drives sales. Onely is not focused on small businesses, local search or paid media. How do you choose the agency whose evidence and delivery plan hold up? Choose the agency whose dated answers, measurement method and delivery plan survive your checks, and confirm the choice with one real test. Send each finalist one real buyer question and request a dated AI answer, a proposed change, its owner, and a date to check the result. Verify the AI-answer evidence down to the raw prompts and responses. Inspect how the agency measures the questions your buyers ask. Trace one change through your approvals to the live page. Sign only for work you can inspect, with a first review and a clean exit. The agency worth hiring is the one that connects your brand to the people asking, and can show you the answers that prove it. What else do people ask about choosing a GEO agency? Is a best-GEO-agencies list enough to build a shortlist? Use a list to find candidates, then request answer-level evidence, measurement methods, a delivery plan, and scope from each. Check whether they can work through your approvals. Can an anonymous GEO case study still be useful? An anonymous case study can qualify if you can inspect dates, methods, changes, and redacted observations or speak to a permitted reference. Which GEO agencies offer a paid pilot before a long contract? Ask every finalist whether it will run a paid pilot before a long contract, because a short, scoped engagement shows how its work moves through your approvals before you commit for a year. Agree the pilot’s prompts, deliverables and review date in writing. How do you check that a GEO agency is brand-safe and compliant before it publishes for you? Check brand safety by asking the agency to show where your product, legal and regional approvers sign off, and to run one draft through that chain during the pilot. Nothing should reach your site or an outside source without a recorded approval. What happens during GEO agency onboarding? Onboarding for a GEO agency should cover access to your CMS and analytics, an agreed prompt set, a dated baseline of AI answers, and a named approver for each kind of change. Ask for that list in the proposal so the first weeks are spent measuring, not waiting for access. Will GEO replace SEO? Keep technical accessibility and useful content in the plan. Add checks of what AI answers say, which sources they cite, and whether they represent your brand accurately. How does a GEO agency work alongside your current SEO agency and digital PR team? A GEO agency should work inside the same data and messaging framework as your SEO agency, content team and digital PR, with a written split of who owns each task. Ask every finalist how its work ties into your current SEO and PR, which changes your in-house team must make, and who reports which result when GEO comes from a second provider, so two agencies never claim the same gain. Should an agency guarantee a place in ChatGPT or Google AI Overviews? Ask for verifiable work and repeated measurement. text: A generative engine optimization agency sells five things: an audit of where you appear in AI answers, a map of what AI systems should know about you, rewritten pages, digital PR, and monitoring. The PR is the part most in-house teams lack; much of the rest you can do with free reports, a writer and a monitoring tool. Search for an agency and you mostly find agency sales pages and "top 10 agencies" lists, usually published by an agency that ranks itself first. Thrad is not a GEO or AEO agency. We sell sponsored, paid placements inside AI conversations, which is a different product, so this is not another list. What is a GEO or AEO agency? A generative engine optimization (GEO) agency, also sold as an answer engine optimization (AEO) agency or AI search agency, works to get a business mentioned, cited and recommended when AI assistants and AI search features answer a buyer's question. Clutch, which lists 30 of them, describes the job as getting businesses "cited and recommended when large language models answer a buyer's question." The labels are interchangeable; our GEO vs SEO and what is AEO guides cover the terms. Judge the agency on its work, not its acronym. Organic or sponsored: which should you be doing? A note on where we stand: Thrad sells sponsored placements inside AI conversations, not agency services. The case for starting with sponsored rests on what the platforms publish, not on our preference. OpenAI states that ads do not influence ChatGPT's answers and that advertisers cannot shape or rank them. Google says there are no special optimizations for AI Overviews or AI Mode beyond being indexed and eligible for a snippet. Nobody can buy a citation. That leaves two separate ways to be present in an AI conversation: Organic: earned and never guaranteed. The model decides, the data you get back is a sample, and movement is measured in months. Sponsored: present the moment the question is asked, in the conversations you choose, labeled as sponsored, with a budget, a schedule and a report you control. Organic work is worth doing, and the rest of this guide covers it straight. But if the question is how to show up in AI conversations this quarter, the controllable answer is sponsored placement. Thrad lets you run one budget across the AI apps your customers already use. Launch a campaign from self-serve . What does a GEO agency actually do? The service pages of Percepture, Directive and Go Fish Digital, three agencies that rank for the term, each describe some version of the same five deliverables: Deliverable What it means In-house? AI visibility audit What it means Where you appear today In-house? Yes, with free reports Entity and topic map What it means What AI should know about you In-house? Partly Page restructuring What it means Direct answers, schema, FAQs In-house? Yes, if you have writers Digital PR What it means Mentions on sites AI cites In-house? Hardest to do alone Monitoring What it means Prompt tracking, reporting In-house? Yes, with a tool Scroll to compare all columns The standard GEO agency scope, from agency service pages observed October 12, 2026. Audit: Percepture describes an audit of current AI visibility, entity presence and content structure. Most of this now comes free from Google Search Console's generative AI reports and Bing Webmaster Tools' AI Performance report. Entity and topic mapping: Directive's process starts here; Go Fish says "we semantically map your entire site to identify how AI systems interpret your authority on key topics." It is keyword research with the question flipped from "what ranks" to "what gets cited." Content restructuring: pages rebuilt with schema, FAQ formatting and direct-answer blocks. Google's guidance is that content should be available in text form and that structured data should match the visible text; there is no AI-specific markup. Digital PR: earning mentions on the sources answer engines draw from. Go Fish states that "citation frequency is one of the strongest predictors of inclusion in AI Overviews." Monitoring: tracking AI mentions, referral traffic and sentiment across a prompt set, usually through the same AEO tools you could subscribe to directly. How much does a GEO agency cost? Most agencies do not publish prices. Those that do, and the guides that survey them, cluster as follows, all as observed on October 12, 2026: Tier Monthly Source Productized packages Monthly $500 to $2,500 Source Digital Elevator guide Mid-market retainers Monthly $2,000 to $10,000 Source Digital Elevator guide Focus Digital Monthly $3,000 to $5,000 Source First Page Sage list First Page Sage Monthly $6,000 to $12,000 Source Its own list Graphite Monthly From $10,000 Source First Page Sage list Enterprise programs Monthly $10,000 to $30,000+ Source Digital Elevator guide Scroll to compare all columns Published GEO and AEO agency prices, October 12, 2026. Digital Elevator's pricing guide says that "most credible AEO/GEO retainers for mid-market businesses land in the $2,000 to $10,000 per month range," with entry-level programs "around $1,000 to $2,500 for basic monitoring and foundational optimization." On Clutch, minimum project sizes run from $1,000 to $50,000 or more, with hourly rates from under $25 to over $300. Hold those against two other numbers: monitoring software costs $50 to $99 a month, and Google and Microsoft's AI reports are free. A retainer should be buying the work those tools cannot do, chiefly content and PR, not the dashboard. Digital Elevator puts citation improvements at three to six months and meaningful results on a six- to twelve-month horizon, so budget for at least two quarters. How do you read an agency's claims? Agency pages lean on numbers. Three tests sort them: Who ranked them? NoGood's list of the best AEO agencies places NoGood first; First Page Sage's list places First Page Sage first, scoring itself on a rubric that rewards publishing prices. A self-published ranking is a brochure. Is the client named? "A tech client saw a 3000% increase in AI mentions in 3 months" cannot be checked. Directive's claim that a named client, Case Status, "went from zero LLM presence to a dominant position across 39+ tracked prompts" within nine months at least gives you the prompt count and the timeframe. Ask for the prompt set. Does it contradict the platforms? Google says of AI Overviews and AI Mode that "there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary." OpenAI says placement in ChatGPT search is not guaranteed . An agency promising proprietary AI placement is selling something the platforms say does not exist. The one controlled study, the 2023 GEO paper , found that adding citations, quotations and statistics lifted visibility in generative answers by 30 to 40 percent on its main metric, that keyword stuffing often made things worse, and that lower-ranked sites gained the most. Any agency's method should be recognizable in that list. What should you ask before signing? Which platforms do you optimize for, and which do you report on? Google AI features and Copilot have free first-party reports; ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity require sampling. Who writes the prompt set, how many prompts, and can we see the raw answers rather than a score? What will you do that our SEO team does not already do? If the answer is schema and FAQs, you may be paying GEO prices for SEO. Which third-party sites will you pitch for mentions, and what have you placed for other clients? How will results show up in Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, not only in your dashboard? What is the minimum term, and what happens to the content and prompt data if we leave? What can you not promise? The right answer includes placement in any specific assistant. When do you need an agency, and when don't you? If you already have an SEO owner, a writer and the free reports, you probably do not. Add a monitoring tool, apply the GEO study's findings to your top pages, and review quarterly. You probably do if nobody owns search, if your category depends on third-party reviews and forums where you have no relationships, or if you operate across several markets and languages. In between, a fixed-scope project, an audit plus a content plan, costs less than a retainer and tells you whether the retainer is worth it. What no GEO agency can sell you Every GEO deliverable earns organic presence over months. None of it can put you in a conversation this week, and none of it is guaranteed. That gap is what sponsored placement fills, and it is the only thing Thrad sells: we are not an AEO or GEO agency and we do not optimize your site. Launch a campaign from self-serve , or read our conversational advertising overview . Considering paid placements alongside organic visibility? Thrad places sponsored ads inside AI conversations. Explore that option separately from work to earn organic citations. Explore sponsored placements A GEO agency checklist Open the free Google and Bing AI reports before taking any agency's audit. Get three proposals and compare scope, not price: platforms, prompts, content volume, PR targets. Discount any ranking the agency published about itself and any result without a named client. Require reporting that lands in your Search Console and analytics, with raw answer text. Start with a fixed-scope audit and content plan; move to a retainer only when it shows movement. text: Summary Choose a generative engine optimization agency by how it picks the questions it tracks, which sources it works on beyond your site, and whether it can show what AI visibility did for pipeline. Good agencies baseline before they promise anything, track the questions buyers really ask, and never guarantee a spot in ChatGPT or AI Overviews. What does a GEO agency actually do? A generative engine optimization agency gets your brand named and linked in the answers ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews give when buyers ask about your category. A GEO agency, also sold as an AEO agency, an LLM SEO agency or an AI search optimization agency, does that by working on the pages and sources those engines read, then measuring which questions you win. A word on who’s writing this. Earleads is a GEO agency, so we sell the thing this guide helps you buy. We don’t rank anyone here. Read it as a rubric, and hold us to it as hard as anyone else on your shortlist, starting with our own generative engine optimization agency page, which answers the same questions. Two facts from Google frame the job. Google says “there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary,” and that a supporting link must be “indexed and eligible to be shown in Google Search with a snippet” ( Google Search Central, AI features ). The same page says AI Overviews and AI Mode “may use a ‘query fan-out’ technique, issuing multiple related searches across subtopics and data sources.” So a GEO agency’s work starts with ordinary search foundations, then widens to every source a fan-out can land on. In practice, AI answers draw on five kinds of sources, and a serious agency will tell you which of the five it touches. We wrote up how AI agents pick what to recommend separately. For choosing an agency, the map below is enough. Five sources feed the answer. Most agencies stop at the answer, before the visit ever reaches your CRM. The bottom half of that picture is where buyers get burned. A citation is a line in a chat window. It isn’t revenue until someone clicks, gets identified, lands in your CRM with an owner, and buys. Before you talk to a GEO agency, write down 3 things If you show up to the first call empty-handed, you’ll leave with the agency’s prompt list, success metric and timeline. Three short notes flip that. The 10 to 20 questions your buyers ask before they buy Pull them from sales call notes, support tickets, review sites, and the threads where buyers compare options. A B2B payroll vendor might write “best payroll software for a 50 person team.” A skincare brand might write “fragrance free moisturizer for sensitive skin.” None of them should contain your brand name. This list is yours, and every agency you talk to should be measured against it, not against a list it wrote. The 2 or 3 numbers that would make this worth it Pick numbers you already track. For a sales-led B2B company that’s often AI-referred demo requests and meetings. For a B2C app or store it’s accounts created or orders. Write today’s value next to each one, even if it’s zero. An agency that can’t say how its work would move one of those numbers is selling you a dashboard. Who on your side approves content fast Every good GEO engagement stalls on approvals at some point. Name one person who can say yes to a draft within a few days. If nobody can, fix that before you sign with any generative engine optimization agency, because the fee keeps running while drafts wait. If you’d rather not build the baseline alone, our free AI visibility audit maps 5 conversion queries in 7 days, shows who wins each one on every engine, and lists the pages and threads the engines read. Bring it to every agency call, ours included. 12 questions to ask a GEO agency (and what good and bad answers sound like) Every guide on how to choose a GEO agency lists questions. Few tell you what a good answer sounds like, which is the only part that helps on a live call. Google’s own page on hiring an SEO is a good template. It suggests asking for past work, asking “What results and timeframe should I expect, and how do you measure success?”, and asking whether every change will be communicated with reasoning. We’ve adapted that to AI answers. 1. Which questions will you track, and who approves the list? A good answer sounds like “We’ll draft the list from your sales calls, reviews, community threads and search data, then you approve every question before we measure anything.” A red flag answer sounds like “We use our standard prompt set,” or a sample list where half the prompts include your brand name. 2. What is our baseline today, by engine? A good answer sounds like “Here’s a citation map per question and per engine, built before we sent the proposal.” A red flag answer sounds like a single AI visibility score with no questions behind it. 3. Which engines do you measure, and how often do you rerun the checks? A good answer sounds like “ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity and AI Overviews, rerun on a fixed schedule, because answers change week to week.” A red flag answer sounds like one engine, or one screenshot from last month. 4. Which sources outside our site will you work on? A good answer sounds like a named list of the practitioner sites, communities, videos and pages the engines already read for your questions. A red flag answer sounds like “We’ll publish more blog posts.” 5. What will you change on our site first, and why? A good answer sounds like “Crawler access and indexing first, then the few pages closest to buying questions.” A red flag answer sounds like a site-wide rewrite, or “schema everywhere” as the whole plan. 6. Who writes the content, and who checks it? A good answer sounds like named writers with domain knowledge, and you approve every piece before it goes live. A red flag answer sounds like a volume promise with unnamed writers and AI-only drafts. 7. How do you connect a citation to pipeline or sales? A good answer sounds like “Tagged AI referrals, identified visits, CRM records with an owner, and revenue reported by engine.” A red flag answer sounds like “Citations are the KPI.” 8. What can you promise, and what can’t you? A good answer sounds like “We promise the work, the cadence and the reporting. Nobody can guarantee placement in an AI answer.” A red flag answer sounds like guaranteed citations, guaranteed rankings or “position 1 in ChatGPT.” 9. What would make you change the plan? A good answer sounds like a stated rule, for example “If a question hasn’t moved after a set number of weeks, we switch to a different source.” A red flag answer sounds like “Trust the process.” 10. Show me one case. What changed, when, and what else happened at the same time? A good answer sounds like dated changes, before and after per question, and honest caveats about what else moved. A red flag answer sounds like a percentage with no baseline and no timeframe. 11. What do you need from us each week? A good answer sounds like a named approver, a short weekly review, and access to analytics and the CRM. A red flag answer sounds like “Nothing, we handle it all.” 12. What do we keep if we stop? A good answer sounds like “The audit, the question list, the content and the tracking setup are yours.” A red flag answer sounds like everything living inside their tool and disappearing with the contract. Questions 1, 7 and 12 do the most work. If a GEO agency answers those three well, the rest of the call is usually detail. If it fumbles question 1, stop there, because every number it reports afterward depends on that list. Red flags that should end the call with a GEO agency Google’s guidance for hiring an SEO is blunt. “No one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google,” and its warning signs include refusing to explain methods and keeping changes secret ( Google Search Central ). Even agencies that publish rankings agree. Digital Elevator writes that “no agency can guarantee that a brand will appear in a specific AI answer, because the platforms control their own models and citation logic and change them frequently” ( Digital Elevator ). End the call, or at least stop taking it seriously, when you hear any of these: Guaranteed citations, rankings or “position 1 in ChatGPT” No baseline before the proposal They chose the prompts and won’t show them, or the prompts contain your brand name One engine only Reporting that ends at mentions or a visibility score A method they can’t explain in plain words, or changes they won’t name in advance Tactics only on your own site, nothing on the sources answers are built from Pricing with no deliverables attached Results promised inside 30 days No exit, with your data and content locked in their platform One more, quieter flag. Watch for a GEO agency that has one playbook for every market. The KDD 2024 GEO paper from Princeton and IIT researchers found GEO methods “can boost visibility by up to 40% in generative engine responses,” and in the same abstract that “the efficacy of these strategies varies across domains, underscoring the need for domain-specific optimization methods” ( Aggarwal et al., KDD 2024 ). The 40% is a research ceiling, not a promise anyone can sell you. The second sentence is the useful one. What works for developer tools won’t automatically work for pet food. Vanity prompts vs buyer prompts A vanity prompt is one written so the dashboard looks good. “Is [Brand] a good tool?” “What does [Brand] do?” “[Brand] reviews.” An engine asked about you by name will usually talk about you, so a report built on those prompts shows high visibility from week one. It also predicts nothing, because buyers who already know your name aren’t the ones you’re trying to reach. A buyer prompt is the question someone asks before they know you exist. “Best payroll tool for a 50 person team.” “Alternative to [incumbent] for ecommerce.” “Is [category] worth it for a small team?” Your share of answers on those questions is low at first and hard to move. That’s exactly why it’s the number worth paying for. If your brand name is in the prompt, the test is rigged. The test takes two minutes. Ask every finalist for the exact prompt list they’d track, then count how many contain your brand name. Our rule is simple. Branded prompts belong in a separate reputation check, and they shouldn’t count toward any visibility number an AI SEO agency reports to you. How much does a GEO agency cost? Published ranges for GEO agency pricing run from about $1,500 a month for small companies to $10,000 a month for most mid-market teams, with enterprise retainers well above that. Three agencies publish numbers on their own pages: WebFX’s GEO pricing guide gives $1,500 to $5,000 a month for small businesses, $5,000 to $25,000 and up for mid-size companies, and $25,000 to $50,000 and up for enterprise. It says its own AI Search Optimization service starts at $3,000 a month. Direct Online Marketing publishes GEO tiers at $3,500 a month, from $6,500 and from $9,500, with working media included in the upper two. Digital Elevator states that most credible mid-market GEO retainers land between $2,000 and $10,000 a month. Five things move the price inside those ranges. How many engines get tracked. How much content gets written, and by whom. Whether community and video work is included or left to you. How much technical fixing your site needs. And whether attribution to your CRM is part of the scope or an extra. Compare fees only after you normalize them. Put each proposal’s deliverables side by side, add the hours your own team will spend approving and supplying input, and divide. A cheaper retainer that eats several hours a week of your head of marketing can cost more than a pricier one that runs on a short weekly review. If a proposal lists a price without deliverables, you can’t run that math at all, which is why it’s on the red flag list. What a good GEO engagement looks like over 6 months A good GEO engagement has a diagnosis you keep, a short sprint against numbers baselined on day one, and a renewal decision made on evidence. Use the timeline below as a buyer’s checklist. It’s also how we run our own engagements, so judge us by it too. Diagnose, sprint on 2 or 3 numbers, decide at day 60, then let the loops compound. Week 0 to 1: a diagnosis you keep The citation map, the sources the engines read for each question, and the question list for your approval. At Earleads this is a paid audit, and you own it whether or not you hire us. Whoever runs it, insist the diagnosis is yours. Days 1 to 60: a sprint on 2 or 3 baselined numbers Not a long list of goals. Two or three, each with a day-one value. A sprint that short forces the agency to pick the few pages, threads and fixes most likely to move them, and it gives you a clean decision point at day 60. Months 3 to 6: the loops compound Checks get rerun every week and the plan adjusts. Our own term is six months, renewable, because month three is the earliest the loops start compounding. A contract much longer than that, with no evidence checkpoint, asks you to pay for faith. A weekly view you’ll actually open One page, every Monday. What shipped, what’s queued, what’s waiting on you. Ours is put together by a GTM engineer, a copywriter and AI agents working the account together, and it’s the same page the client sees. B2B vs B2C: what changes when you hire Search results for this topic split into B2B SaaS lists and ecommerce lists. The questions to ask a GEO agency are the same for both, but the prompts, the sources and the success metric aren’t. B2B: committees and comparisons B2B buyers ask committee questions and comparison questions. “Alternative to [incumbent] for a mid-size sales team.” “Does [category] integrate with Salesforce?” A good B2B GEO agency works the practitioner articles and communities where those comparisons happen, and it measures success in pipeline and meetings, not traffic. Ask it to show you how an AI-referred visit becomes a named account in your CRM. B2C and ecommerce: products and reviews B2C buyers ask product, review and “best for me” questions. “Best running shoes for flat feet.” “Is [brand] worth it?” Communities and video carry more weight here, and so does product feed readiness. A good GEO agency for ecommerce reports accounts created and orders, and it can talk about your product data, not just your blog. GEO agency, SEO agency or in-house? Pick on two things. Who already owns your search foundations, and whether anyone on your side can work off-site sources and attribution every week. Google’s point that AI features run on the same foundations as search means a strong SEO setup isn’t wasted. It’s the floor, not the whole job. Option Pick it when Watch for GEO agency You need multi-engine tracking, off-site source work and attribution, and nobody in-house has time for all three Vanity prompts, reporting that stops at citations, no exit terms SEO agency adding GEO Your SEO agency already performs and will commit to buyer questions and multi-engine reporting in writing GEO as a relabeled SEO retainer with an AI visibility score bolted on In-house team You have a writer with domain depth, someone who can participate in communities, and analytics access Nobody owning the reruns, so measurement quietly stops after a few months Whichever you choose, the technical floor is the same. OpenAI says “OAI-SearchBot is used to surface websites in search results in ChatGPT’s search features” and that “sites that are opted out of OAI-SearchBot will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers” ( OpenAI, bots ). GPTBot, the training crawler, is separate. Perplexity says PerplexityBot “is designed to surface and link websites in search results on Perplexity” and isn’t used to train foundation models ( Perplexity, bots ). Check your robots.txt for both before you pay anyone. Measurement has a floor too. ChatGPT adds utm_source=chatgpt.com to the links it sends from search results, according to OpenAI’s publishers and developers FAQ , so ChatGPT referrals are easy to separate in your analytics. Google is different. Sites in AI features “are included in the overall search traffic in Search Console,” inside the normal Web report ( Google Search Central ). So when an agency shows you “AI Overview traffic from Search Console,” ask how it was separated out, because Google doesn’t split it for you. Should you trust “best GEO agency” lists? Use them to build a longlist, not to decide. Most ranked lists of the best GEO agencies on page one are published by an agency, and the publisher usually sits in first place. Some of those lists are well researched, but a ranking written by a vendor can’t tell you which generative engine optimization agency fits your buyers. The 12 questions and the scorecard below work better, because they apply the same test to every agency, including whoever wrote the list you found them on. Fill one column per finalist after each call. What to compare Strong answer Weak answer Agency A Agency B Prompt selection Drafted from your buyers, approved by you Their standard set, or branded prompts Baseline Citation map per question and engine before the proposal A single visibility score Engines ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, AI Overviews One engine Off-site sources Named communities, sites and videos “More blog posts” Content team Named writers, you approve Unnamed writers, AI-only drafts Attribution to CRM AI referrals traced to records and revenue by engine Citations as the KPI Reporting cadence Weekly, one page Monthly deck, or on request What you keep Audit, question list, content, tracking Everything stays in their tool Published price Price tied to deliverables Price with no scope Guarantee language Promises work and reporting only Guarantees citations or rankings An agency that wins most rows on the strong side is worth a second call. An agency that lands on the weak side for prompt selection or guarantee language isn’t, whatever it scores elsewhere. Get a personalised case study Pick your industry and we'll email you the case closest to your business, numbers included. Sent. Your case study is on its way. Frequently asked questions How much does a GEO agency cost? Published ranges start around $1,500 a month for small companies and reach $25,000 to $50,000 and up for enterprise, according to WebFX's own GEO pricing guide. Digital Elevator puts most credible mid-market retainers between $2,000 and $10,000 a month. The fee alone tells you little, so ask each agency what every tier delivers and how much of your team's time it needs. Can a GEO agency guarantee I get cited in ChatGPT? No. OpenAI, Google, Perplexity and Anthropic decide what their engines cite, and they change how they do it. Google's own advice on hiring an SEO says no one can guarantee a #1 ranking, and the same logic applies to AI answers. A good GEO agency promises the work, the cadence and the reporting, never a placement. How long until a GEO agency shows results? Ask for a baseline on day one and 2 or 3 numbers to move within the first 60 days. That's enough time to see whether the work is landing on the questions you picked. Compounding usually takes months, because off-site sources and new pages take time to be read and reused, so treat any promise of results inside 30 days with caution. Is a GEO agency different from an SEO agency? Partly. Google says its AI features rely on the same foundations as search, with no special optimization required, so solid SEO still matters. A GEO agency adds three things most SEO agencies don't run by default. It tracks buyer questions across several AI engines, works on the off-site sources answers draw from, and reports on citations and AI referral traffic. What should a GEO agency deliver? A GEO agency should deliver a baseline citation map per question and engine, a question list you approve, technical fixes so crawlers like OAI-SearchBot and PerplexityBot can read your pages, content and off-site work on the sources answers draw on, and a weekly report that ties AI referrals to visits, CRM records and pipeline. What is the best GEO agency for B2B SaaS or ecommerce? The best GEO agency for B2B SaaS or ecommerce is the one that tracks your buyers' real questions and can show dated results on similar ones. Most ranked lists of GEO agencies are written by an agency that places itself first. Run every finalist through the same 12 questions and the scorecard instead, including the agency that wrote the list.
